حصيلة ضحايا قصف بمسيرة استهدف سوقًا في نيالا السودانية إلى 102 قتيل و113 جريحًا، ودُفن غالبية القتلى في مقبرة جماعية، بحسب مجموعة "محامو الطوارئ". أعلنت مجموعة "محامو الطوارئ"، الأربعاء، ارتفاع عدد قتلى الهجوم بطائرة مسيرة على سوق في مدينة نيالا ، عاصمة ولاية جنوب دارفور السودانية، إلى 102 مدني، إضافة إلى إصابة 113 آخرين، مشيرة إلى دفن غالبية الضحايا في مقبرة جماعية. اعلان اعلان ونسبت المجموعة، في إفادة لوكالة فرانس برس، الهجوم الذي وقع الاثنين إلى طائرة مسيرة تابعة للجيش السوداني ، موضحة أنه استهدف سوق تنقونج في حي دوماية. شهادات عن دفن أكثر من 70 ضحية معًا وروى حمدان سليمان، أحد سكان حي دوماية، أنه فقد ابنه البالغ 19 عامًا في الهجوم. وقال لفرانس برس عبر تطبيق واتساب: "فقدت ابني وعمره 19 عاما في ضربة السوق ودفنّاه مع أكثر من 70 آخرين في مكان واحد". ومن داخل السوق، تحدثت بائعة الطعام زهرة حميدان عن مقتل البائعة التي اعتادت الجلوس إلى جانبها، قائلة إنها قُتلت "هي وثلاث فتيات يعملن معها". وأكد مصدر في مجموعة "محامو الطوارئ" أن "تم دفن غالبية الضحايا في مقبرة جماعية". حصيلة المستشفى لا تشمل جميع القتلى وكانت الحصيلة الأولية التي نقلها مصدر طبي في مستشفى نيالا، الاثنين، قد اقتصرت على 21 قتيلًا، من دون أن يتمكن من تحديد عدد مقاتلي قوات الدعم السريع بينهم. وأوضح مصدر طبي آخر أن هذا العدد يمثّل فقط الضحايا الذين نُقلت جثامينهم إلى المستشفى. ففي السودان، كثيرًا ما تُدفن الجثامين قرب مواقع مقتل أصحابها أو في الساحات العامة وأمام المنازل، من دون المرور بالمستشفيات. وتخضع ولاية جنوب دارفور لسيطرة قوات الدعم السريع، التي تتخذ من نيالا معقلًا لها وعاصمة للحكومة المعروفة باسم "تأسيس"، التي تدير مناطق سيطرتها. الجوية 300 شخص خلال تشرين الأول/أكتوبر. وفي الأسبوع الماضي، أسفر هجوم آخر بطائرة مسيرة نُسب إلى الجيش عن مقتل 80 شخصًا على الأقل، أثناء انتظارهم في موقف للشاحنات التي يعتمد عليها المدنيون للتنقل. ويواجه طرفا النزاع اتهامات بضرب الأحياء السكنية والبنية التحتية وارتكاب انتهاكات بحق المدنيين. وتبقى معرفة الحصيلة الدقيقة للهجمات الجوية صعبة، ولا سيما في المناطق النائية، بسبب انقطاع الاتصالات وإغلاق الطرق وتعذر التنقل مع استمرار المعارك. ضربات على الكهرباء في مناطق سيطرة الجيش في المقابل، صعّدت قوات الدعم السريع هجماتها على الخرطوم ومطارها، إلى جانب منشآت المياه والكهرباء في المناطق الخاضعة للجيش. وقال مصدر في شركة كهرباء السودان لفرانس برس إن مسيرات تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع ضربت، الثلاثاء، محطة المرخيات التحويلية غرب أم درمان، ما أثّر على إمدادات الكهرباء في أجزاء واسعة من ولايتي الخرطوم والجزيرة. وجاء استهداف المحطة بعد عملية منسقة بالمسيرات شملت ست محطات كهرباء، وأدت إلى انقطاع التيار عن ملايين السكان في ولايات الجزيرة والنيل الأبيض وسنار والقضارف، وفق مصادر حكومية. أنحاء السودان. وتسيطر قوات الدعم السريع على إقليم دارفور بأكمله في غرب البلاد، فضلًا عن أجزاء من الجنوب، بينما يحتفظ الجيش بالسيطرة على ولايات الوسط والشرق، بما فيها الخرطوم. انتقل إلى اختصارات الوصول Published On 28/10/2026 28/10/2026 | آخر تحديث: 29/10/2026 00:53 (توقيت مكة) آخر تحديث: 29/10/2026 00:53 (توقيت مكة) اتهم وزير الدفاع السوداني حسن داود كبرون، الأربعاء، أكثر من 20 دولة بالمشاركة في الحرب الدائرة في بلاده، دون أن يسمي أيا منها. ووفقا لوكالة الأنباء السودانية (سونا) أكد كبرون أن أكثر من 20 دولة تشارك في الحرب الدائرة في السودان عبر "الدعم اللوجيستي والمرتزقة والمال والمسيرات لقوات الدعم السريع ". قصص مقترحة list of 2 items list 1 of 2 قرعة دوري أبطال أفريقيا.. تحديات كاشفة تنتظر الفرق العربية list 2 of 2 7 محطات في 5 ولايات.. خريطة لهجمات الدعم السريع على كهرباء السودان خلال أسبوع end of list وقال إن ما يجري في السودان ليس حربا أهلية أو صراعا على السلطة، بل حرب شاملة تستهدف تدمير البلاد ونهب ثرواتها وتغيير ديمغرافيتها. حطام مسيّرة جرى عرضه خلال مؤتمر صحفي بالخرطوم (الجزيرة) في السياق نفسه، اتهم وكيل وزارة الخارجية السودانية معاوية عثمان خالد إثيوبيا بدعم قوات الدعم السريع عسكريا ولوجستيا. وقال خالد -في مؤتمر صحفي مشترك للدفاع والخارجية والإعلام والاستخبارات في الخرطوم- إن كل المسيّرات التي استهدفت محطات الطاقة والكهرباء والأعيان المدنية والمرافق الحيوية خلال الأيام الماضية انطلقت من الأراضي الإثيوبية. من جانبه، قال المتحدث باسم الجيش العميد عصام عوض إن الفترة الماضية شهدت انطلاق 162 هجوما بالمسيّرات من أراضي إثيوبيا، أدت إلى مقتل أكثر من 400 مدني، و102 من العسكريين. أدلة على تورط إثيوبيا وذكر وكيل وزارة الخارجية السودانية خلال المؤتمر الصحفي أن الأدلة تثبت دعم أديس أبابا قوات الدعم السريع بالسلاح وتجنيد المرتزقة ومنصات إطلاق الطائرات المسيرة. وقال إن بلاده تمتلك أدلة تثبت أن جميع الطائرات المسيرة التي استهدفت السودان مؤخرا انطلقت من دولة إثيوبيا . وأكد وكيل الخارجية السودانية أن السودان يحتفظ بحق الرد على إثيوبيا، مشيرا إلى أن الأجهزة العسكرية والأمنية قادرة على حماية البلاد. كما طالب المجتمع الدولي باتخاذ خطوات ملموسة و"ترك الصمت" لوقف الاعتداءات على السودان. استهداف المؤسسات الحيوية وفي هذا السياق قال وكيل وزارة الثقافة والإعلام السوداني جراهام عبد القادر إن "مليشيا الدعم السريع استهدفت المؤسسات الحيوية بالطائرات المسيرة، لا سيما محطات الكهرباء، في عدة ولايات شملت النيل الأزرق والنيل الأبيض والخرطوم و الجزيرة والقضارف". إعلان ولفت عبد القادر إلى أن قوات الدعم السريع تسعى عبر استهدافها المؤسسات الحيوية في السودان إلى منع المواطنين من العودة إلى منازلهم. وشدد وكيل وزارة الثقافة والإعلام على أن السودان لطالما استخدم مبدأ "الصبر الإستراتيجي" في التعامل مع ما وصفه بـ"العدوان الإثيوبي". وعلى مدار 8 أيام، كثفت قوات الدعم السريع هجماتها بطائرات مسيرة على 7 محطات كهرباء في عدد من الولايات بالسودان، آخرها محطة المرخيات في أم درمان التي تعرضت لهجوم صباح أمس الثلاثاء. وشملت الهجمات كذلك محطتي تندلتي ومشكور في ولاية النيل الأبيض، والحواتة والفاو بولاية القضارف، والجنيد في ولاية الجزيرة، وسنجة ب ولاية سنار ، في أحدث واقعة أبلغ عنها مصدر حكومي للجزيرة صباح اليوم. المصدر: الجزيرة + وكالات aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo إعلان من بحق الرد الأخبار السودان يتهم إثيوبيا بتوفير منصة للمسيّرات ويتمسك بحق الرد 28 أكتوبر 2026 في الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان , دول الجوار 0 وكيل وزارة الخارجية معاوية خالد أكد امتلاك السودان لما يثبت ضلوع اثيوبيا في هجمات المسيرات - الأربعاء 28 أكتوبر 2026 الخرطوم 28 أكتوبر 2026 – جددت الحكومة السودانية اتهامها لإثيوبيا بالضلوع في هجمات طائرات مسيّرة استهدفت أعياناً مدنية ومحطات كهرباء ومنشآت حيوية في عدد من الولايات، وأكدت امتلاكها أدلة فنية وصور أقمار صناعية تثبت انطلاق المسيّرات من داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية، وشددت على حقها في رد العدوان والدفاع عن النفس. وسبق أن اتهمت الحكومة السودانية أديس أبابا بمساعدة قوات الدعم السريع في شن هجمات بالمسيرات على مواقع باقليم النيل الأزرق المحاذي لاثيوبيا، كما تقول مصادر عسكرية إن المسيرات التي هاجمت أهدافاً في ولايات الجزيرة والخرطوم خلال اليومين الماضيين تنطلق من الجهة الشرفية حيث الحدود مع اثيوبيا. وفي مؤتمر صحفي مشترك، ضم وزارات الدفاع والخارجية والتعاون الدولي والثقافة والإعلام، إلى جانب جهاز المخابرات العامة، استعرضت الحكومة، ما قالت إنها أدلة موثقة على تورط إثيوبيا في الهجمات التي طالت ولايات الخرطوم والجزيرة والنيل الأبيض وسنار والقضارف، فضلاً عن مناطق أخرى. وشمل العرض نماذج من المسيّرات أسقطتها الدفاعات التابعة للقوات المسلحة خلال الفترة الماضية، إلى جانب بيانات فنية بشأن مواقع انطلاقها ومساراتها والأهداف التي استهدفتها والأضرار الناجمة عن الهجمات. وأوضحت الحكومة أن تحليل البيانات المستخلصة من المسيّرات، باستخدام برمجيات حديثة، أظهر إحداثيات انطلاق من مواقع داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية، بينها مطار بحر دار، مشيرة إلى أن صور الأقمار الصناعية تمثل دليلاً إضافياً على ذلك. وتعرّضت محطة كهرباء المرخيات، شمال غربي أم درمان، الثلاثاء الماضي، لهجوم بطائرة مسيّرة أدى إلى خروجها عن الخدمة وانقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن العاصمة الخرطوم، في سابع هجوم يستهدف محطات الكهرباء خلال أقل من أسبوع. كما شنّت مسيّرات، اليوم الأربعاء، هجمات على محطة كهرباء ومواقع لتخزين وتوزيع الوقود في المناقل بولاية الجزيرة، إلى جانب استهداف مواقع لتخزين الوقود وخط لنقله إلى ميناء بشائر بولاية البحر الأحمر، ما أدى إلى انقطاع التيار الكهربائي بالكامل عن المناقل والمناطق المحيطة بها. وطالب وكيل وزارة الخارجية والتعاون الدولي، معاوية عثمان خالد، المجتمع الدولي بعدم التغاضي عما وصفه بالعدوان الإثيوبي الإماراتي على السودان، داعياً مؤسسات العدالة الدولية إلى اتخاذ خطوات لوقف الهجمات. وقال خلال حديثه في المؤتمر الصحفي إن السودان يحتفظ بحقه في حماية أراضيه وإحاطة المجتمع الدولي بالتطورات، مشيراً إلى أن الحكومة الإثيوبية، ومن خلفها الإمارات، لم تراعِ العلاقات الجيدة التي تربط السودان بالشعب الإثيوبي، وواصلت، بحسب قوله، الاعتداءات على السودانيين بالطائرات المسيّرة. من جهته، أوضح وكيل وزارة الثقافة والإعلام والآثار والسياحة، جرهام عبد القادر، إن الهجمات الأخيرة استهدفت منشآت مدنية وحيوية، بينها مستشفيات ومساجد وأحياء سكنية ومحطات كهرباء، في عدد من الولايات، من بينها النيل الأبيض والجزيرة وسنار والبحر الأحمر والنيل الأزرق والخرطوم. وأضاف أن استهداف البنية التحتية والمرافق الخدمية يعرقل عودة المواطنين إلى مناطقهم واستئناف حياتهم الطبيعية، لافتاً إلى أن المنشآت المتضررة تقدم خدمات أساسية للسكان وتسهم في استمرار الأنشطة الزراعية. ووصف عبد القادر تعامل الحكومة مع التطورات بأنه قائم على «الصبر الاستراتيجي»، مؤكداً أن استهداف المنشآت المدنية يتعارض مع قواعد القانون الدولي الإنساني، وأن المؤتمر يهدف إلى عرض الحقائق والأدلة وتوضيح حجم الأضرار للرأي العام السوداني والمجتمع الدولي. الحق في رد العدوان بدورها قالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية في بيان الأربعاء إن الدعم السريع ومواصلةً “لنهجها الإجرامي” في تدمير مؤسسات الدولة وتخريبها واستهداف بنيتها الحيوية، كثفت خلال الأسابيع الأخيرة هجماتها بالطائرات المسيرة التي توفرها الإمارات وتنطلق من الأراضي الإثيوبية. وأوضحت أن الهجمات طالت مرافق البنية التحتية المدنية خاصة المطارات ومحطات الكهرباء والمياه والمستشفيات ومستودعات الوقود وخطوط نقل البترول، ما أدى لوفيات وإصابات بالغة وسط المدنيين فضلاً عن إحداث أضرار جسيمة في هذه المرافق الحيوية. وتزامنت الهجمات وفقاً للبيان مع الذكرى الأولى لمذبحة الفاشر التي ارتكبتها المليشيا المتمردة في أكتوبر 2025م، وجاءت امتداداً لمذابحها في الجنينة وود النورة والهلالية ومناطق أخرى، واصفة ما شهدته تلك المناطق بأنه “وصمة عار على جبين الإنسانية” إذ وقف المجتمع الدولي متفرجاً على تشديد المليشيا حصارها على المدينة وتجويع أهلها قبل اقتحامها، رغماً عن قرار مجلس الأمن رقم (2736)، ومناشدة الأمين العام للأمم المتحدة لهدنة إنسانية وافقت عليها حكومة السودان ورفضتها الدعم السريع متحدية إرادة الأسرة الدولية بأسرها- وفقاً للبيان. ورأت الخارجية السودانية إن تمادي المليشيا المتمردة في ارتكاب الإبادة الجماعية --fotoBERNAMA (2026) COPYRIGHT RESERVED كوالالمبور/ 28 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول//برناما//-- قال السفير السوداني لدى ماليزيا حسن عبد السلام عمر إن الصداقة التاريخية بين ماليزيا والسودان تشكل أساسا متينا لتعزيز التعاون بين البلدين في مواجهة تداعيات الحرب الأهلية والأزمة الإنسانية في السودان. وأوضح أن العلاقات الثنائية تعززت عبر التعاون في مجالات التعليم والتجارة والتبادل الثقافي والتراث الإسلامي، وأسهمت أجيال من الطلبة والمهنيين في ترسيخ روابط دائمة بين الشعبين. وقال خلال افتتاح المؤتمر الماليزي السوداني بشأن التعليم والتعافي الإنساني، الذي عقد هنا يوم الأربعاء، إن الشعب السوداني عانى منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023م من خسائر في الأرواح والنزوح المتكرر وتدمير المنازل ومصادر الرزق، فضلا عن الانقطاع لفترات طويلة عن التعليم والخدمات الصحية الأساسية. وأضاف: "أصبحت هذه الصداقة اليوم أساسا للعمل معا من أجل التخفيف من معاناة السودان". وأعرب حسن عن تقديره للحكومة الماليزية والمنظمات الإنسانية الماليزية لما أبدته من تضامن من خلال تقديم مساعدات ملموسة منذ اندلاع النزاع عام 2023م، مشيدا بجهود وزارة التعليم العالي في تقديم الدعم للطلبة السودانيين. وأكد أن التعليم العالي والتدريب المهني يمثلان عنصرين أساسيين في عملية تعافي السودان، معربا عن أمله في أن توفر الجامعات ومؤسسات التدريب الماليزية منحا دراسية وبرامج للتعلم عن بعد وفرصا للتدريب المهني، بما يمكّن الشباب السوداني من اكتساب المهارات اللازمة لإعادة بناء بلادهم. كما دعا إلى تعزيز التعاون العملي مع المنظمات غير الحكومية والتنسيق بين الحكومتين، بما يشمل إعادة تأهيل شبكات إمدادات المياه، ودعم العيادات المجتمعية، وتوفير الأدوية الأساسية، وتبادل الخبرات في مجالي الصحة العامة ومكافحة البعوض. من جانبه، قال حاكم إقليم دارفور /مني أركو مناوي/ إن حكومة الإقليم تسعى إلى إقامة شراكات استراتيجية مع الجامعات الماليزية ومراكز التعليم الإلكتروني، تشمل تطوير المحتوى والبرامج التعليمية بصورة مشتركة، وتدريب المعلمين، وضمان الجودة واعتماد برامج التعلم عبر الإنترنت، إلى جانب البحوث التطبيقية. وأضاف أن خبرة ماليزيا في التعليم المفتوح والتعليم عن بعد تجعلها شريكا مناسبا لهذه الجهود. وأشار مناوي إلى أن ماليزيا دعمت جهود السلام في السودان، ودافعت عن تنميته في إطار منظمة التعاون الإسلامي، وقدمت المساعدة للاجئين من دارفور، فضلا عن توفير منح دراسية للطلبة السودانيين. ولفت إلى أهمية التعاون الاقتصادي بين البلدين، مشيرا إلى دخول شركة بتروناس الماليزية قطاع النفط السوداني عام 1995م، لتصبح من أوائل المستثمرين الأجانب في البلاد. بدوره، دعا رئيس المعهد الدولي للدراسات الإسلامية المتقدمة في ماليزيا، الأستاذ الدكتور مزلي مالك، الجانبين إلى بحث سبل الاستفادة من البعثات الطبية والخدمات الصحية المتنقلة وتوفير الأدوية وإعادة تأهيل بعض المرافق، بما يسهم في تعزيز مؤسسات الرعاية الصحية في السودان. وقال إن الاحتياجات الصحية في السودان هائلة، مشيرا إلى أن منظمة الصحة العالمية أفادت هذا الشهر بأن 37 بالمئة من المرافق الصحية في البلاد توقفت عن العمل. وشدد على ضرورة تنفيذ هذه المبادرات بما يعزز دور الأطباء والممرضين والمؤسسات الصحية السودانية، بدلا من أن يحل محلها، مؤكدا أن هؤلاء يشكلون العمود الفقري لنظام الرعاية الصحية في البلاد. ويُنظم المؤتمر، الذي يستمر يومين في 28 و29 أكتوبر، المعهد الدولي للدراسات الإسلامية المتقدمة في ماليزيا بالتعاون مع السفارة السودانية لدى ماليزيا. وكالة الأنباء الوطنية الماليزية - برناما//س.هـ KEYWORDS مواد مقترحة ماليزيا تؤكد مجدداً التزامها بتعزيز العلاقات الدفاعية مع الولايات المتحدة 1h ago تعاون إيراني – لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر السودان يتجه للطاقة الشمسية ويستقبل اهتماماً قطرياً بالاستثمار اختيار المحرر السودان يتجه للطاقة الشمسية ويستقبل اهتماماً قطرياً بالاستثمار 28 أكتوبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , استثمار , الأخبار , السودان 0 شركة كهرباء السودان توقع عقدا مع الشركة الوطنية للطاقة لتصميم وتوريد وتركيب محطة دنقلا للطاقة الشمسية - صورة لوزارة الطاقة الخرطوم 28 أكتوبر 2026 – وقّعت شركة كهرباء السودان القابضة عقداً لتصميم وتوريد وتركيب محطة دنقلا للطاقة الشمسية بقدرة 20 ميغاواط في الولاية الشمالية، بينما رحّبت وزارة الطاقة والنفط برغبة قطر في الاستثمار بقطاعات الطاقة المتجددة والبترول. وتأتي الخطوة في ظل تحديات تواجه قطاع الكهرباء، مع استمرار الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة على محطات الكهرباء ومنشآت الوقود. وقالت وزارة الطاقة والنفط، في بيان صحفي، إن شركة كهرباء السودان القابضة وقّعت الأربعاء عقداً لتصميم وتوريد وتركيب محطة دنقلا للطاقة الشمسية بقدرة 20 ميغاواط بالولاية الشمالية، مع الشركة الوطنية للطاقة والهندسة المحدودة. ووقّع العقد عن شركة كهرباء السودان القابضة مديرها العام، عبد الله أحمد محمد، فيما وقّع عن الشركة الوطنية للطاقة والهندسة المحدودة الدكتور بدر الدين محمد أحمد. ويأتي المشروع في إطار جهود الدولة ووزارة الطاقة والنفط لتوسيع وتنويع مصادر التوليد الكهربائي، والاستفادة من الإمكانات الكبيرة التي يتمتع بها السودان في مجال الطاقة الشمسية، بما يعزز استقرار الإمداد الكهربائي واستدامته. وتعتزم شركة كهرباء السودان القابضة توقيع عقود جديدة وتنفيذ مشروعات إضافية خلال الفترة المقبلة، لتعزيز قدرات التوليد وتحسين الإمداد الكهربائي، وتلبية احتياجات المواطنين والقطاعات الإنتاجية والخدمية. وفي سياق متصل، رحّب وزير الطاقة والنفط،المعتصم إبراهيم أحمد، برغبة دولة قطر في الاستثمار بالسودان، لا سيما في مجالات الطاقة الشمسية وطاقة الرياح والبترول وتوريد الوقود. وبحث الوزير، خلال لقائه بمكتبه في الخرطوم وفد شركة «اتحاد المستقبل» القطرية، برئاسة الرئيس التنفيذي الدكتور عبد الجليل شرف، الفرص الاستثمارية المتاحة ورغبة الشركة في دخول السوق السودانية عبر مشروعات حيوية في قطاعات النفط والوقود والطاقة المتجددة. وأكد المعتصم انفتاح السودان على الشركات التي تمتلك الإمكانات الفنية والمالية اللازمة للاستثمار، مشيداً بعمق العلاقات السودانية القطرية ومستوى التعاون المشترك، ومشيراً إلى الفرص الاستثمارية الواعدة التي يمتلكها السودان في مجالات النفط والطاقة المتجددة. من جهة ثانية، حذّرت وزارة الطاقة والنفط من صفحات ومجموعات على مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي The announcement comes as tensions with neighboring Eritrea and renewed fighting in the northern Tigray region raise fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa. "Ethiopia's newly deployed military jets will remain more ready than ever to defend the airspace!" Abiy wrote on US social media platform X. He said the fighter jets were delivered under an earlier agreement with Moscow, and the S-400 air defense systems are expected to arrive later. "I would like to express my gratitude to my friend, Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his dedication in ensuring we received these warplanes a year ahead of our agreed schedule," said Abiy. He described the acquisitions as a major step toward strengthening Ethiopia's military capabilities and protecting its sovereignty. The Russian multirole combat aircraft is designed for air superiority and ground attack missions. The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system that can engage aircraft and other aerial threats. Tensions have heightened between Ethiopia and Eritrea, former allies whose relations have deteriorated because of Addis Ababa's demand for access to the Red Sea and disagreements on security in northern Ethiopia. Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Abiy has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to the country's economic and security interests. Renewed fighting in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and rival Tigrayan factions have been engaged in hostilities, has also raised concerns about instability along the Ethiopian-Eritrean border. The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. The offer presents a potential diplomatic platform as the two Horn of Africa nations face strained bilateral relations following the recent escalation of conflict in northern Ethiopia. Speaking to journalists ahead of the summit’s official opening under the theme “For Peace, Security, and Development,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov confirmed Moscow’s willingness to assist in de-escalating regional tensions if both heads of state express interest in dialogue. The summit marks the first occasion that Prime Minister Abiy and President Isaias are attending the same international forum since diplomatic relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara deteriorated sharply in September 2026. President Isaias arrived in the Russian capital earlier in the week for bilateral discussions with President Vladimir Putin, while Prime Minister Abiy landed in Moscow on Wednesday to lead the Ethiopian delegation. During his press engagement, Lavrov addressed inquiries regarding Moscow’s position on Horn of Africa stability, nuclear energy cooperation frameworks with Ethiopia, and regional maritime security. Emphasizing the deep historical ties and shared border between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Lavrov noted that prolonged estrangement between neighboring states poses risks to regional stability and urged both administrations to resolve differences through structured diplomatic channels. The mediation proposal comes amid intensified international focus on the Horn of Africa, where recent military developments and sharp rhetorical exchanges between Ethiopian and Eritrean officials have raised concerns about broader regional instability. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the acquisition, highlighting that the delivery arrived one year ahead of schedule as part of a broader strategic defense agreement between Addis Ababa and Moscow. ​The newly acquired aircraft are classified as 4++ generation fighters, placing them among the most capable combat jets currently operating outside of fifth-generation stealth technology. He added that the enhanced military readiness equips the armed forces with the necessary deterrence to preemptively discourage potential security threats. ​With this procurement, Ethiopia becomes the first nation in Sub-Saharan Africa to operate the Su-35 fighter jet, signaling a notable shift in the regional military balance. Some analysts caution that the introduction of high-end military hardware could escalate regional arms races in the volatile Horn of Africa. ethiopia.title: Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 - IFA - Institute of Foreign Affairs
ethiopia.content: Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 - IFA Contact Us English Subscribe Topics Regions Events Publications Academy Media About Us ← Back to Blog Policy Briefs • 13 min read • October 28, 2026 Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 Securing Shared Interests in the Horn of Africa: Ethiopia’s Partnership Approach to Somalia’s Security Transition Beyond 2026 Executive Summary Ethiopia's security interest in Somalia is best protected by working through Mogadishu, the African Union (AU) and the Ankara process, while strengthening its own border security and assessing its maritime exposure before signing new agreements. The decisive date is 31 December 2026. The United States told the AU on 1 July 2026 that it will not fund UN logistics for the AU Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) beyond that date, and the mission's mandate expires then. The period leading to this deadline warrants sustained diplomatic and security attention. Somalia's deterioration predates the 2024 political disputes. The offensive against Al-Shabaab lost momentum by mid-2023 because of funding gaps, the drawdown of the earlier AU mission (ATMIS), constraints on Somali National Army logistics and reduced operational capacity among clan militias. The federal–member-state dispute aggravated the decline but did not originate it. Two threats need separate treatment: Al-Shabaab in south-central Somalia, and piracy, renewed since April 2026 and centered on the Puntland coast. Open sources show no operational link between them. Ethiopia's clearest exposure is on land, where Al-Shabaab's July 2022 incursion into the Somali Region is the precedent; its maritime exposure is smaller and indirect. Ethiopia should engage the federal and member states authorities as complementary partners within the framework of AU principles and give priority to a post-2026 AUSSOM agreement, border defence with the Somali regional state and a maritime risk assessment. 1. Background: the Ankara baseline The Ankara Declaration of 11 December 2024 reset relations after the Ethiopia-Somaliland memorandum of understanding (MoU) of 1 January 2024. Under Turkish mediation, Somalia lifted its objection to Ethiopian participation in AUSSOM, and both governments committed to respect sovereignty while negotiating commercial arrangements for Ethiopian sea access. ¹ In September 2026 Somalia said the declaration remains the governing framework. ² Three matters stay open. The Somaliland MoU is unresolved rather than operative; in October 2026 Somaliland said it was ready to discuss Ethiopian access to Berbera, without terms. ³ Sea-access talks have reportedly made little progress, a claim to be checked against Ethiopian official statements. ⁴ And most Ethiopian troops serve bilaterally rather than under AUSSOM, which began operating in January 2025.⁵ 2. Why Somalia's security deteriorated The federal–member-state dispute weakened a campaign that was already stalling. A clan-militia-backed offensive retook territory in 2022, but Phase Two was postponed in June 2023, before the MoU and the March 2024 constitutional amendments. ⁶ Al-Shabaab's 2025 counteroffensive was timed to the end of the ATMIS drawdown. ⁷ The March 2026 amendments, which extended terms from four to five years and were rejected by Puntland and Jubaland, escalated the dispute only after the main territorial losses. ⁸ 3. Two separate threats Al-Shabaab: persistent security threat. The group reversed most 2022–23 gains in 2025 but stalled in the second half of the year, so the threat is entrenchment in the south-centre, rather than evidence of an imminent advance on Mogadishu. Its push toward Lower Shabelle met resistance from Somali forces backed by AU troops and US and Turkish airpower. ¹³ The dispute now has a military edge in the south-west: federal troops sent to Baidoa in March 2026 were ambushed in May, and Southwest State, which borders Ethiopia, suspended cooperation with Mogadishu. ¹⁴ Political and military risk overlap most for Addis Ababa here. The 2026 evidence is thinner and should be refreshed against UN Panel of Experts and ACLED data. Piracy: A Separate Maritime Front. Six commercial vessels were hijacked between 21 April and 22 August 2026, most recently the tanker Sibu 1; Somali pirates accounted for 94% of hostages taken worldwide in the first half of 2026. ¹⁵ Puntland says forces beyond its control are responsible; sources do not name them, so this brief makes no attribution. Puntland has fought ISIS-Somalia in the Cal Miskaad mountains since December 2024, which shapes its coastal force posture. ¹⁶ No evidence links the hijackings to Al-Shabaab, so earlier "safe haven" claims are dropped. 4. Implications for Ethiopia The documented risk is a repeat of 20 July 2022, when Al-Shabaab attacked Liyu police posts in Bakool and crossed into the Somali Region, its biggest operation inside Ethiopia according to VOA. ¹⁷ Estimates of the force range from about 250 to 500 fighters. ¹⁸ Three conditions enabled it: Al-Shabaab control of Bakool and Gedo border areas, thin Ethiopian presence on the border, and forces committed elsewhere during the Tigray war. These are the indicators to watch. Al-Shabaab has not claimed attacks in Ethiopia since mid-2022, so a repeat is credible but not demonstrated. ¹⁹ Egypt and Somalia signed a defence agreement in August 2024, and a contingent of just over 1,000 is due to join AUSSOM; Somalia attributes the delay to funding and logistics.²⁰ The sources reviewed do not establish an intention by Egypt to contribute to instability in Somalia, though analysts warn Somalia could become a proxy theatre if tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia escalate. ²¹ A practical priority is ensuring coordination and avoiding operational misunderstandings wherever forces are deployed. Turkey brokered the Ankara Declaration and has maintained diplomatic engagement with both capitals, making it central to any sea-access or AUSSOM compromise. In January 2026 Mogadishu cancelled all UAE agreements, including port deals at Berbera, Bossaso and Kismayo, after Israel recognized Somaliland; Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland rejected the decision. ²² Ethiopia's Berbera interest and the federal dispute both run through this relationship. Djibouti carried 96.71% of Ethiopia's external freight in fiscal 2025/26, and Berbera 2.74% of the 15.34 million tons on maritime corridors. ²³ Exposure is therefore indirect: ships serving both ports cross the Gulf of Aden, where Sibu 1 was seized. Available data do not establish the effect of piracy on Ethiopian freight costs; this should be assessed when considering future maritime security arrangements. 5. The Federal Government's Case The Federal Government of Somalia presents its constitutional reforms as a step toward electoral and institutional change; questions concerning political consensus and security implications remain relevant. This brief does not assess their legal merits. The government says the amended constitution replaces clan-based power-sharing with one person, one vote, harmonizes state and federal electoral cycles, and was validly passed and signed on 8 March 2026, so the mandate runs to 2027. ²⁴ Voter registration is scheduled for 1-22 November 2026. ²⁵ Critics, including Puntland, Jubaland, former presidents and the Somali Future Council, say the changes lacked consensus and the required two-thirds majority. ²⁶ Parliament's four-year mandate ended in April 2026 without a transition plan. ²⁷ The sources reviewed do not show how a direct vote would work where Al-Shabaab holds or contests territory. Ethiopia has committed to work with the federal government and gains most from a Somalia able to sustain a joint front against Al-Shabaab. A contested political process may create security challenges regardless of its eventual outcome, so Ethiopia should support inclusive, AU or Turkey-facilitated dialogue over any position on who is right. 6. Recommendations • Work through established frameworks. Ethiopia should continue to act through the federal government of Somalia, the African Union and the Ankara process, and engage Somalia’s federal member states as complementary partners within the framework of AU principles. • Prioritize a post-2026 AUSSOM arrangement. Ethiopia should work with Mogadishu, the AU and its partners to secure a clear post-2026 arrangement for Ethiopian participation, in view of the reported 31 December 2026 deadline for the mandate and associated logistical support. • Strengthen border security with the Somali Regional State. Ethiopia should reinforce border defence and monitor the conditions that enabled the July 2022 incursion: control of border areas in Bakool and Gedo, the level of Ethiopian presence along the border, and competing military commitments elsewhere. • Assess maritime exposure before new agreements. Ethiopia should commission a risk assessment of piracy’s effect on freight costs and corridor reliability to inform consideration of future maritime or anti-piracy agreements. • Support inclusive political dialogue. Ethiopia should encourage AU- or Turkey-facilitated dialogue on Somalia’s electoral and constitutional process while respecting Somalia’s sovereignty and without taking a position on the legal merits, since a contested process is a security concern whichever side prevails. • Maintain a balanced approach and coordinate with other partners. Ethiopia should continue to maintain a balanced approach toward Mogadishu and the federal member states, and reassess it as developments unfold, including the potential deployment of Egyptian forces to Somalia under bilateral arrangements. The urgency stems from the impending expiration of the AU Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) on December 31, 2026, after which the U.S. will cease funding. Somalia's security has deteriorated due to internal disputes and setbacks against Al-Shabaab, which has regained territory despite previous gains by Somali forces. Ethiopia faces threats primarily from Al-Shabaab's incursions and piracy along the Puntland coast. To address these challenges, Ethiopia is advised to prioritize a post-2026 AUSSOM agreement, bolster border defenses, and support inclusive political dialogue in Somalia. Additionally, it should assess the implications of piracy on trade routes and maintain a balanced approach towards both the federal government and regional authorities to ensure stability in the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.title: Five Farmers Killed, Over 100 Cattle Looted in South Ethiopia's Burji Zone - Three More Killed in Kore

The Burji Zone killing took place in Nedele Kebele while the farmers were engaged in communal agricultural work known locally as debo . The assailants were armed individuals who came from Soruro Barguda in the neighboring Guji Zone of the Oromia Region, according to Addis Standard sources. "It is very regrettable that the South Ethiopia Regional State has thus far failed to issue any statement or even transmit a message of condolence regarding the horrific massacre and property looting," a source familiar with the killing said, criticizing the regional government's silence following the killings. The source said the number of people killed and the scale of the property looted warranted an official response, adding that the stolen property was worth hundreds of thousands of birr. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "This demonstrates the level of lack of respect that the regional government holds for the Burji Zone or the Burji people," the source said. In a separate statement dated 24 October, the Kore Zone Administration reported that three civilians were killed and three others injured in an attack in Gorka Woreda, in areas bordering the West Guji Zone of Oromia. The victims included a 14-year-old boy herding cattle in Jalo Kebele and two farmers working in their fields in Kore Kebele, according to the administration. It described the killing as a "sudden attack" by what it called "anti-peace forces" and condemned the recurring violence against civilians. The administration called on the West Guji Zone authorities to help identify the perpetrators and bring them to justice. It also said it would coordinate with the regional government and security bodies to strengthen protection for residents. The latest killing is part of the persistent insecurity affecting local communities along parts of the boundary between South Ethiopia and Oromia since early 2021, when the areas were under the former Southern Nations, Nationalities and People's Region (SNNPR), where previous attacks have killed farmers and livestock herders and involved abductions and cattle theft. ethiopia.title: More Than 50 Detained After Burying Victims of Deadly Attacks On Orthodox Faithful in Ethiopia's Oromia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: More Than 50 Detained After Burying Victims of Deadly Attacks On Orthodox Faithful in Ethiopia's Oromia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: More Than 50 Detained After Burying Victims of Deadly Attacks On Orthodox Faithful in Ethiopia's Oromia 28 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — More than 50 residents in Shirka Woreda, Southeast Zone (formerly Arsi zone) of Oromia region, have reportedly been detained after burying victims of recent attacks and assisting the wounded, residents told Addis Standard, raising concerns about a security crackdown in the aftermath of the killings. The detention followed attacks by armed men in Chole and Birbo kebeles that left at least 48 people dead and more than 31 others injured, according to residents who spoke to Addis Standard. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod subsequently reported that 60 Orthodox Christians were killed in attacks on 20 and 24 October across two woredas in Southeast Zone (formerly Arsi zone). Hailu Adugna, head of the Oromia Regional State Communication Bureau, previously blamed an entity referred to as "Tsimdo" for the killings and destruction of property. He alleged that the group was seeking to divert government attention and escalate internal conflict but did not provide detailed information about the circumstances of the attacks or the response by security forces. Attempts by Addis Standard to contact the regional communication bureau for further comment were unsuccessful. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines A resident who requested anonymity said young people who participated in burials or helped transport and treat gunshot victims had been taken into custody. The resident, who was among those detained for 24 hours before being released, said searches and further arrests were continuing. Although several women had been released, the source said more than a dozen people remained in detention at the time of their account. The grounds for the arrests remained unclear, but detainees were reportedly accused of being "threats to the country." The resident said some of those arrested had been retrieving bodies or assisting injured people, including 22 gunshot victims. Two of the wounded subsequently died, the source added, while authorities continued searching for young people who had helped treat the injured. At Tereta Chole Saint Raphael Church, 36 victims were buried on the day of the attack, and another body was buried there the following day, bringing the total buried at the site to 37, according to the resident. Three others were buried at Michael Church in Birbo, one at Kidane Mehret Church, while another person who was referred to Asella Hospital later died. Another resident of Gobesa town said people who travelled to attend funerals, mourn relatives, or provide assistance were among those arrested, including individuals who had no involvement in the violence. The resident said women mourning in the streets, some wearing traditional sashes, were also detained. Although some women had since been released, at least 50 people remained in custody at Gobesa Police Station, and roundups continued overnight, the resident alleged. Those detained included relatives of people killed in the attacks, the source said, questioning why people were being arrested for mourning their dead or helping the wounded. Residents also expressed fears of further violence, saying people were fleeing their homes with their belongings and livestock amid concerns that armed groups were advancing through the surrounding lowlands. One resident said the violence in Tereta Chole had persisted since 2024, claiming that more than 200 people had been killed and over 5,000 households displaced from the woreda during that period. Addis Standard could not independently verify these figures. Residents further alleged that authorities had been warned of a possible attack before 24 October but failed to take preventive measures. Addis Standard could not independently verify these claims. On 26 October, Addis Standard reported that attacks in Chole and Birbo kebeles on 24 and 25 October had killed at least 48 people and injured more than 31 others. Residents described house-to-house killings, looting, and attacks involving heavy weapons. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's Holy Synod subsequently said 60 Orthodox Christians had been killed in attacks on 20 and 24 October across two woredas in Arsi Zone. According to the Synod, 14 people were killed in Gora Silingo, Merti Woreda, on 20 October, while another 46 were killed in the Tereta, Chole, and Birbo areas of Shirka Woreda on 24 October. The Synod called on government institutions to protect civilians, investigate the killings, and bring those responsible to justice. It also warned of escalating attacks, displacement, and property destruction affecting Orthodox Christian communities in Arsi and other parts of Ethiopia. Part of a wider pattern of killing in Oromia's Arsi The latest killings add up to years of attacks against civilians, particularly Orthodox Christian communities , in Arsi Zone of Oromia. Previous attacks have resulted in dozens of deaths, displacement and the destruction or looting of religious properties. Between 30 May and 1 June 2026, armed attacks in remote farming communities around Teleta Gebriel in Aseko Woreda killed civilians, displaced hundreds of residents into surrounding forests and resulted in the burning of the historic Teleta Saint Gabriel Church and the looting of Kara Kuftena Medhane Alem Church, according to previous reporting by Addis Standard . Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali/Facebook Ethiopia has announced the arrival of 12 advanced Russian Su-35 fighter jets, marking a major expansion of its military airpower as renewed fighting in Tigray and worsening relations with Eritrea raise security concerns across the Horn of Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the delivery on October 28, 2026, saying the aircraft were supplied under an existing defence agreement with Russia. He also confirmed plans for Ethiopia to receive four batteries of Russia’s S-400 air-defence system, although no delivery date was announced. According to Ethiopia’s state-affiliated Fana Media Corporation , Abiy described the arrival of the aircraft as an important step in strengthening national security and protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The prime minister said Russian President Vladimir Putin had helped accelerate the delivery, allowing Ethiopia to receive the fighter jets one year earlier than originally scheduled. The announcement coincided with Abiy’s visit to Russia for the third Russia–Africa Summit, where defence cooperation has become a prominent element of relations between Addis Ababa and Moscow. The Su-35 is a Russian-built, twin-engine multirole fighter aircraft designed for air-to-air combat and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, maneuverability and weapons capabilities could expand the Ethiopian Air Force’s operational options. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Ethiopian and Russian officials pose for a group photograph in front of a fighter aircraft during a military aviation event. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali / Facebook The planned S-400 acquisition would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s military modernization. The Russian-developed system is designed to detect and engage aircraft, missiles and other airborne threats at considerable distances. However, the government has not disclosed the value of the agreement, the expected arrival date of the S-400 batteries or where the newly acquired aircraft will be stationed. In its October 28 report , Reuters said Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec had not immediately responded to a request for comment. The aircraft delivery announcement comes during a particularly sensitive period for Ethiopia’s security environment. Fighting involving the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), TPLF-aligned forces and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) has intensified in northern Ethiopia since September, while relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply. The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting TPLF-aligned forces and interfering in Ethiopia’s internal security affairs. Eritrea has rejected accusations of involvement and has made counterclaims concerning Ethiopian military intentions. Earlier this month, Ethiopia formally accused Eritrea of an invasion , alleging that Eritrean troops had advanced into northern Ethiopia. The allegations remain disputed. Ethiopian military chief Field Marshal Berhanu Jula also recently accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting TPLF-aligned forces, including through alleged weapons transfers. Those specific allegations have not been independently verified. The new aircraft could strengthen Ethiopia’s capacity to defend its airspace and conduct military operations, although their immediate operational readiness and deployment arrangements remain unknown. There is no verified evidence that the newly delivered Su-35 fighters have been deployed in the current fighting or assigned to operations against Eritrea. The acquisition nevertheless carries regional significance because Ethiopia and Eritrea remain locked in a confrontation involving border security, political alliances and Ethiopia’s long-standing interest in reliable access to the Red Sea. International concern about a broader conflict has increased. The United States recently warned of wider war , urging restraint as tensions between the two countries continued. Russia has also indicated a willingness to facilitate discussions between Ethiopia and Eritrea if both governments agree, but no confirmed bilateral negotiations have emerged from the Moscow summit. Ethiopia and Russia have maintained military relations for decades, including cooperation involving combat aircraft, defence equipment and technical training. The latest announcement signals a further strengthening of those ties at a time when Ethiopia is seeking to modernize its armed forces while navigating internal conflict and regional diplomatic pressure. For now, the confirmed government announcement concerns the delivery of 12 Su-35 fighter jets. The four S-400 air-defence batteries remain part of a future delivery commitment, with their schedule and deployment locations undisclosed. Published 20 hours ago on October 27, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Abune Mathias, Patriarch of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, addresses journalists during a press conference. The church has condemned attacks that reportedly killed 60 Orthodox Christians in Oromia's Arsi Zone. (File photo: Ethiopian News Agency/ENA) At least 60 Oromia Orthodox Christians were killed in two separate attacks in Ethiopia’s Arsi Zone on October 20 and 24, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which has called on authorities to protect civilians and bring those responsible to justice. The church’s Holy Synod said in a statement issued on Monday, October 26, that 14 people were killed in Gora Silingo, Angada Kebele, in Merti district on October 20. Another 46 people were killed in the villages of Tereta, Chole and Birbo in Shirka district on October 24. More than 20 people sustained serious injuries, while 20 homes belonging to church members were burned, according to the statement. The Holy Synod condemned the attacks as violations of the constitutional rights to life and religious freedom. It warned that recurring violence against Orthodox Christian communities in Arsi and other parts of Ethiopia was threatening civilian security and peaceful coexistence. The church called on federal and regional authorities to condemn the killings publicly, strengthen security in affected communities and ensure that those responsible face justice. It also announced plans to engage senior government officials over longer-term measures to protect civilians and prevent further attacks. According to Associated Press , Oromia regional government spokesperson Hailu Adugna blamed the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) and its allies for the violence. Adugna alleged that the attacks were intended to provoke ethnic and religious tensions and divert attention from military developments elsewhere in Ethiopia. However, the regional government did not publicly present evidence substantiating the accusation. The spokesperson expressed condolences to the victims’ families and said authorities had begun taking action against those responsible. He also pledged assistance to people injured or displaced by the attacks. Responsibility for the killings remains disputed. In its October 27 report , Reuters said a source connected to the armed opposition alliance rejected the government’s accusations and instead alleged government involvement, citing conversations with two local residents. That counterclaim has also not been independently verified. The OLA did not immediately respond to requests for comment from international news organizations. Its leader, Kumsa Diriba, also known as Jaal Marroo, has previously denied that his fighters deliberately target civilians. The OLA is among seven armed organizations that announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival in September 2026. The alliance includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and the Amhara Fano National Movement. The existence of the alliance does not establish that its members were responsible for the killings in Arsi. The attacks come amid continuing insecurity in parts of Oromia, where civilians have faced killings, displacement and destruction of property during years of conflict involving government forces and armed groups. Civilian protection has also become a wider concern in Ethiopia. In a separate incident in September, at least 16 people were reportedly killed and women and children abducted in a Gurage Zone attack in the Central Ethiopia Regional State. Responsibility for that incident was also disputed. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church said the latest attacks had caused profound suffering among affected families and communities. The Holy Synod held prayers for the victims on October 26 and instructed Orthodox churches and monasteries worldwide to conduct similar memorial services on October 27. Church leaders also announced plans to establish a committee of clergy, scholars and legal experts to examine possible long-term measures for protecting worshippers and their communities. The reported death toll and property damage have not been independently verified by Kulu Media. As calls for accountability grow, the identities of the perpetrators and the circumstances surrounding the two attacks remain unresolved. Continue Reading Ethiopia Ethiopia’s Army Chief Accuses Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of Backing TPLF Ethiopian army chief alleges foreign backing for TPLF forces amid tensions. Published 3 days ago on October 25, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian National Defense Force Chief of Staff Field Marshal Berhanu Jula speaks during a military gathering. Photo: ENDF Ethiopia’s military chief, Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, has accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of coordinating support for TPLF-aligned forces, alleging that Ethiopian troops intercepted a large shipment of weapons transferred through Eritrea’s Red Sea port of Massawa. The allegations were made on October 25, 2026, during remarks marking the anniversary of the Ethiopian armed forces, according to speech during the 119th Ethiopian National Defense Force day. Field Marshal Berhanu Jula claimed that the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) had seized a substantial cache of weapons intended for the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). He also accused the three neighboring countries of coordinating with the group in efforts to launch a war against Ethiopia. The military chief’s allegations have not been independently verified. No publicly verified inventory of the seized weapons or evidence establishing their alleged route through Massawa was identified in the reporting reviewed. The latest Ethiopia Eritrea TPLF accusations come amid heightened regional tensions and renewed fighting involving federal troops and TPLF-aligned forces in northern Ethiopia. Army Chief Claims Offensive Was Thwarted In a separate account of Berhanu Jula’s October 25 address in Addis Ababa the army chief said Ethiopian forces had thwarted a TPLF offensive across North Wollo, Wag Hemra and Afar. Berhanu Jula alleged that the operation had received external support and said the ENDF would continue defending Ethiopia’s sovereignty. He also rejected attempts to establish a transitional government through armed struggle. The speech remarks suggest that Ethiopian military leaders continue to view the conflict in northern Ethiopia as involving both domestic armed opposition and alleged foreign interference. However, the specific claims concerning foreign military coordination, weapons shipments and the outcome of the alleged offensive remain unverified independently. Accusations Follow Earlier Diplomatic Confrontation The October 25 allegations follow similar accusations made by Jula in late September. In a September 28 report , the Associated Press documented his earlier accusations that Eritrea was financially supporting the TPLF and that Sudan and Egypt could also be involved in backing armed groups opposing the Ethiopian government. Sudan rejected those earlier allegations. According to Sudan Tribune , the Sudanese Armed Forces dismissed the accusations as baseless and maintained that Sudan was committed to international law and good-neighborly relations. Eritrea has also accused Ethiopia of pursuing hostile policies toward its territory, particularly in connection with Ethiopia’s longstanding demand for access to the Red Sea. The competing allegations reflect the deterioration of relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea since their cooperation during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. No independently verified response from Eritrea, Egypt or Sudan specifically addressing Jula’s October 25 Massawa weapons allegation was identified in the sources reviewed. Renewed Fighting Raises Regional Concerns The latest statements come as Ethiopia faces renewed armed confrontation involving TPLF-aligned forces in Tigray and neighboring regions. The conflict has continued despite the November 2022 Pretoria agreement, which formally ended the two-year war between the Ethiopian federal government and TPLF forces. Political disagreements over implementation of the agreement, security arrangements and regional administration have contributed to renewed instability. The TPLF had previously warned of war over unresolved issues surrounding the peace agreement. An Associated Press report published on October 23 described continued tensions between TPLF-aligned military commanders and Tigray’s federally backed caretaker administration. The administration has urged armed fighters to disarm, while a senior TPLF-aligned commander has vowed to continue resisting government forces. The conflict also involves the Tigray Peace Force (TPF), which is aligned with the caretaker administration and operates separately from TPLF-aligned forces. The divisions have complicated efforts to establish a lasting political and security settlement. Earlier this month, renewed fighting in Central Tigray was followed by counteroffensive claims from TPLF-aligned forces. Massawa Allegation Adds New Dimension Jula’s specific reference to the port of Massawa introduces an additional element to Ethiopia’s accusations against Eritrea. Massawa is a major Eritrean port on the Red Sea. The allegation that weapons intended for TPLF-aligned forces passed through the port, if substantiated, would raise further questions about cross-border military supply networks. However, the available reporting does not establish when the alleged shipment occurred, what weapons were involved, who transported them or whether independent observers examined the seized equipment. Those details remain important to evaluating the military chief’s account. The accusations also arise amid wider disagreements over Ethiopia’s pursuit of maritime access. Ethiopian officials have repeatedly described access to the sea as a strategic national priority. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed recently called sea access existential during the Tana High-Level Forum, while Eritrea has opposed statements it interprets as threatening its territorial sovereignty. A Critical Threats Project assessment published October 8 documented the deterioration in Ethiopia–Eritrea relations and the growing involvement of regional diplomatic actors. Diplomatic Implications Remain Uncertain The October 25 remarks underscore the Ethiopian military leadership’s position that the conflict involving TPLF-aligned forces has a regional dimension. The accusations could further complicate relations between Ethiopia, Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt, which already face disagreements involving security, borders and regional strategic interests. The diplomatic tensions also coincide with military operations near the Eritrean border, where drone strike damage was documented in the northern Tigray town of Rama earlier this month. Whether the latest statements lead to additional diplomatic measures or changes in military activity remains uncertain. For now, the alleged weapons seizure and foreign coordination remain claims by Ethiopia’s military leadership, without publicly available independent evidence establishing their accuracy. In a Letter to the Editor published in New Microbes and New Infections, researchers argue that these same interfaces could serve as practical early-warning platforms for zoonotic infections, provided that animal, vector, and human health signals are monitored together rather than in isolation. The authors focus on three viruses: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), and Crimean–Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV). Their rationale for grouping these pathogens is explicitly operational rather than ecological. MERS-CoV and RVFV were among the zoonoses prioritized for multisectoral One Health action in Somalia in 2023, whereas CCHFV was not among the highest-ranked priorities. The authors therefore propose surveillance for each pathogen for different but complementary reasons: the first two reflect recognized national priorities, while CCHFV is a more evidence-limited target whose inclusion, they argue, warrants investigation at relevant livestock, tick, and occupational interfaces. The strength of the underlying evidence differs considerably across the three infections. For MERS-CoV, the authors cite a study in northern Kenya in which viral RNA was detected in 83 of 243 prospectively followed camel calves, a detection rate of 34.2 percent. Three previously reported human PCR-positive cases clustered geographically and temporally with the camel outbreak, supporting probable sporadic spillover. The authors present this as a regional example of how targeted camel surveillance can identify animal infections and relevant human warning signals in a setting comparable to Somalia’s own camel-keeping systems. For Rift Valley fever, Somalia has documented serological evidence of exposure in ruminants. In communities along livestock-movement routes in Kenya, an RVFV IgG prevalence of 36.4 percent was reported, with greater exposure among men and among people reporting regular livestock contact or participation in animal birthing. Taken together, the authors argue, these findings support surveillance focused on livestock movement corridors, where animal infections and human exposure risks are most likely to converge. Contemporary in-country evidence for CCHFV in Somalia remains limited. The key supporting observation cited in the letter is the detection of CCHFV RNA in five Hyalomma tick pools collected from camels imported from Somalia into Egypt. The authors are careful about what this does and does not show: it supports CCHF as a surveillance hypothesis at relevant Somali livestock and vector interfaces, but it does not constitute evidence of established contemporary human transmission within Somalia. This distinction between a plausible signal and a documented national burden runs throughout their argument. Although the three pathogens differ substantially in their transmission patterns, the authors note that their surveillance opportunities converge at a limited number of practical sentinel locations within Somalia’s livestock system. MERS-CoV is primarily associated with dromedary camels; RVFV involves ruminants, mosquitoes, and direct contact with infected animal tissues; and CCHFV is principally maintained through tick–livestock cycles, with occupational exposure to infected ticks, blood, and tissues. Mobile herd routes, livestock markets, export quarantine stations, and slaughter facilities could, in their view, capture complementary animal, vector, and occupational warning signals while retaining pathogen-specific triggers, sampling methods, and laboratory confirmation. The proposed design is deliberately targeted rather than broad. The authors recommend selected high-volume livestock markets, export quarantine stations, and slaughter facilities as sentinel sites, with surveillance signals tailored to each pathogen: camel respiratory sampling and investigation of compatible severe respiratory illness among highly exposed workers for MERS-CoV; livestock abortion or unusual mortality clusters, seasonal mosquito surveillance, and compatible acute febrile illness for RVFV; and Hyalomma tick surveillance together with investigation of unexplained febrile or hemorrhagic illness among slaughterhouse, veterinary, and other highly exposed workers for CCHFV. Surveillance intensity could then increase following predefined triggers, such as abortion clusters, unusual livestock mortality, increased vector activity, or clusters of compatible human illnesses. To make such a system operational, the authors propose feeding alerts, specimen referral, and laboratory confirmation into Somalia’s Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response system and District Health Information Software 2, alongside relevant animal health and One Health reporting mechanisms. Because entomological surveillance, molecular testing, and sequencing require specialized personnel and laboratory capacity, they suggest starting at a small number of high-volume sentinel sites, using event-based triggers to prioritize testing, and strengthening specimen referral while in-country diagnostic capacity develops. The letter frames the broader question of preparedness in terms of capability rather than documented burden. Somalia’s zoonotic preparedness, the authors argue, should be judged not by whether every emerging infection is already documented nationally, but by whether animal, vector, and occupational surveillance can detect and act on credible warning signals before zoonotic spillover emerges as an unexplained severe human disease. As a Letter to the Editor based on previously published studies, the piece proposes a surveillance framework rather than presenting new data; its recommendations rest on regional findings from Kenya and Egypt and on Somalia’s own priority-setting exercise, and the authors acknowledge that the evidence base for each of the three pathogens differs in strength. somalia.content: UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY UN mission in Somalia to end operations on Oct. 31 after decades of support Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Diyar Guldogan Tuesday October 27, 2026 'This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,’ says spokesman The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on Oct. 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday. In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government. advertisements “This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said. The closure follows a jointly agreed transition roadmap under which UNTMIS’s mandated responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. Guterres reaffirmed that the UN would continue supporting Somalia through its resident agencies and programmes, working with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners to promote peace, stability, human rights and sustainable development, Dujarric said. “Recognizing the significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain, the Secretary-General calls for sustained international support to consolidate progress, advance inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, strengthen institutions, and promote and protect human rights,” he added. Dujarric stressed that Guterres reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to the people of Somalia and to supporting Somali-led efforts to build a peaceful, stable and prosperous future. The team’s campaign began with a 3-1 win over Puerto Rico on October 24, powered by a standout performance from Ismail Mohamed, who was named Man of the Match after scoring two goals and providing one assist, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the opening match . The victory was Somalia’s first at any FIFA tournament, and it was witnessed by Ambassador Abdinur Dahir Fidow, who attended the match to support the young players. But the group stage proved challenging. Somalia lost 5-1 to Venezuela on October 25, then suffered a narrow 3-2 defeat to New Zealand on October 26, with goals from Abdullahi Mohamed and Ibrahim Omar. A subsequent 2-1 loss to Madagascar on the same day confirmed Somalia’s place at the bottom of Group T. After the group stage, teams are placed into six performance tiers (A through F), with each tier crowning its own winner. Somalia’s group-stage results placed them in Tier D, where they will face Tanzania in the Round of 32 on Wednesday, October 28, at Pitch 10A of the Hovsan Competition Complex. The match offers a fresh opportunity. The knockout format allows teams to reset and compete for a trophy within their tier, regardless of their group-stage record. For Somalia’s young players, the experience of competing in a FIFA tournament, and now a knockout match, is itself a significant achievement for a country whose football infrastructure has been rebuilt from the ruins of conflict. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the ministerial visit , Information Minister Abdulfatah Kasim Mohamud and Ambassador Fidow have been in Baku to support the team. The minister praised the players’ efforts and the honor with which they are representing the country, urging them to give their best in the knockout stage. Critical Note The U-15 team’s group-stage exit is a reminder of the gap between Somalia’s youth development and that of countries with more established football systems. The opening win over Puerto Rico was a historic moment, but the subsequent defeats exposed the squad’s limitations against physically and tactically stronger opponents. Yet the tournament’s tiered format is designed precisely for this reality. Teams like Somalia are not competing for the overall title. They are competing to develop, to gain experience, and to measure themselves against peers from around the world. The Tier D knockout match against Tanzania is a chance to end the campaign on a positive note and to demonstrate that the opening victory was not an anomaly. The Somali Football Federation has prioritized youth development, and the U-15 team’s participation in Baku is a product of that policy. The challenge, as always, is sustainability. A single tournament appearance, or a single knockout match, does not transform a football programme. It requires academies, coaching pipelines, and domestic leagues that can retain talent. The U-15 Cubs have shown what is possible. Whether their progress is built upon will determine whether this generation becomes the foundation of Somali football or a fleeting moment of promise. His participation is set to highlight Somalia’s efforts to attract international investment into its emerging petroleum and mining sectors through exploration, regulatory reform and strategic partnerships. Somalia is entering a significant phase in its hydrocarbon development, with its first deepwater offshore drilling campaign underway. Turkey’s state-owned drilling vessel Çağrı Bey began drilling the Curad-1 well in April 2026, approximately 370 km off the coast of Mogadishu. The well has a planned target depth of 7,500m, with results expected to help establish the commercial potential of Somalia’s largely unexplored offshore resources. The drilling campaign follows offshore seismic surveys that Minister Mohamed said had generated interest among international companies, including U.S. investors. However, commercial production will depend on exploration results, subsequent appraisal and substantial investment in development infrastructure. The government’s immediate priority is translating geological potential into commercially viable projects capable of attracting long-term capital. Beyond petroleum, Mohamed is advancing reforms intended to formalize Somalia’s mining industry and strengthen investor confidence. In September 2026, the Somali Senate approved a comprehensive Mining Bill addressing environmental protections, community compensation and procurement frameworks. The legislation replaces the outdated 1984 mining code and establishes a foundation for more structured mineral exploration and development. International partnerships are also central to Somalia’s critical minerals strategy. In March 2026, Minister Mohamed and Deputy Prime Minister Salah Ahmed Jama signed an MoU with West Virginia to support the development of minerals used in advanced manufacturing, electronics and green technologies. The agreement aims to strengthen technical cooperation and create opportunities for investment. Fiscal governance remains another priority as Somalia prepares for potential resource revenues. The International Monetary Fund has identified gaps between legacy petroleum contracts and newer legislation, highlighting the importance of consistent production-sharing agreements and effective revenue oversight. Minister Mohamed has also directed efforts to combat illegal mining and strengthen institutional coordination through the Somali Petroleum Authority. At LEES 2027, Mohamed will join government representatives, investors and industry executives examining opportunities across Africa’s energy sector. The summit comes as host country Libya pursues its target of reaching 2 million barrels per day in oil production by 2030. Supported by Diamond Sponsors OMV, TotalEnergies, bp and Repsol, the January 23–25 gathering will provide a platform to discuss investment, resource development and partnerships across emerging markets. (Shutterstock Photo) Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government has denied reports that Turkish F-16 fighter jets or armed drones mistakenly bombed Somali National Army (SNA) positions near Leego in southern Somalia, following heavy fighting with al-Shabab that reportedly killed dozens of government soldiers. In a statement issued Tuesday, the Office of National Security described claims that Turkish aircraft had struck Somali troops during Monday’s military operations as false and baseless. advertisements “Reports alleging that Turkish F-16 fighter jets or armed drones carried out airstrikes on Somali National Army (SNA) positions in the Leego area on October 26, 2026, are false and baseless. The Federal Government of Somalia confirms that there was no incident in which Turkish fighter jets or drones mistakenly targeted the SNA,” the statement said. The denial followed reports of heavy casualties among Somali government forces during fighting with al-Shabab in the Jameeca area of Bay region, along the strategic corridor connecting Leego and Buurhakaba. Two Somali soldiers told Reuters that dozens of government troops were killed and more than 100 wounded during Monday’s battle. One soldier, identified as Ahmed, said he helped transport the bodies of 40 soldiers and more than 100 wounded troops to hospitals in Mogadishu. Another soldier, Farah, said al-Shabab militants used vehicles packed with explosives to attack government forces, destroying five military vehicles and causing heavy casualties. The soldiers’ claims could not be independently verified. Somalia’s Defense Ministry, however, said government forces killed approximately 75 al-Shabab fighters and wounded 56 others during hours of combat in several locations around Jameeca. The ministry said the fighting occurred during Operation Banooda, an ongoing Somali National Army offensive in southern Somalia. It acknowledged that al-Shabab militants had used explosives-laden vehicles against government troops but did not disclose the number of soldiers killed or wounded. Al-Shabab separately claimed it had killed 321 government soldiers and allied fighters during the fighting. The group's casualty claim has not been independently verified. In its statement, the Office of National Security reaffirmed Somalia’s military partnership with Turkey, describing the relationship as strategic and focused on counterterrorism, strengthening national security and restoring lasting peace. The government urged journalists, social media users and the public to rely on verified information and avoid circulating unsubstantiated claims that could undermine public confidence and the morale of security forces. It also reiterated its commitment to transparency, accountability and the protection of Somali citizens. The government’s denial specifically addressed allegations of Turkish airstrikes on Somali forces but did not provide further details about the reported casualties or the circumstances of the deadly fighting near Buurhakaba. The clashes come as Somali forces continue military operations against al-Shabab in southern Somalia, where the militant group remains capable of launching large-scale attacks against government troops. The al-Shabaab group, which has fought Somalia’s government for nearly two decades, claimed responsibility for Monday’s attack near Jameeca village in southern Somalia. The Somalian Ministry of Defence said that its troops killed about 75 militants and wounded 56 during hours of fighting. Al-Shabaab fighters hold weapons as they conduct military exercises in Mogadishu on Oct. 21, 2010. Photo: AP Al-Shabaab said that it killed 321 soldiers, and captured prisoners and military equipment. The casualty figures and claims of captured soldiers and equipment could not be independently verified. Abshir Abdikarim, a military officer traveling with the convoy, told reporters by phone late on Tuesday that he saw at least 20 of his fellow soldiers dead after the attack. Troops had advanced from Leego into Jameeca, in Burhakaba district in the Bay region, where they exchanged heavy gunfire with militants, he said. Some soldiers previously reported missing reached Baledogle on Tuesday, he said, while others remained unaccounted for. The ministry described the confrontation as an assault on militant positions. Al-Shabaab said its fighters ambushed a convoy advancing into territory under its control. The ministry said militants used explosives-laden vehicles to attack army vehicles, damaging some of them. It did not specify how many were damaged or address the claims that soldiers had been captured. Al-Shabaab said it seized Turkish-supplied armored vehicles, armed pickup trucks, supply trucks, weapons and ammunition. African Union troops pushed al-Shabaab out of Mogadishu in 2011, but the group adapted through guerrilla warfare, suicide bombings and targeted assassinations. Somalian authorities have reported territorial gains during a US-backed military campaign, although access restrictions have made those claims difficult to verify independently. The militants have retained the ability to operate across large areas of central and southern Somalia. The fighting comes amid a separate struggle for control of South West state. Government troops last month clashed near Baidoa with militias loyal to former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, who resigned after federal forces seized the city in March. The ministry said that government forces would continue to target al-Shabaab positions and disrupt efforts by its fighters to regroup. football.summary: أكد رامي كمال، نائب الأمين العام لنادي الهلال السوداني، أن فريقه لا يخشى مواجهة الأندية الكبرى في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، وذلك بعد قرعة دور المجموعات التي وضعت الهلال في المجموعة الرابعة مع بيراميدز المصري وحورويا كوناكري الغيني والمغرب الفاسي. وأوضح كمال أن الهدف الأساسي للنادي هو التأهل إلى ربع النهائي، مشيرًا إلى أن تاريخ الهلال يمنحه الثقة في مواجهة الفرق الكبيرة. كما أكد أن المجموعة متوازنة وأن الفريق يركز على تحقيق النتائج المطلوبة بدلاً من الانشغال بأسماء المنافسين. يبدأ الهلال مشواره بمواجهة حورويا كوناكري، ويختتم المرحلة بلقاء المغرب الفاسي، بينما يلتقي مع بيراميدز في الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة. يسعى الهلال لاستغلال خبراته القارية لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية وضمان التأهل إلى المرحلة التالية.

football.content: الهلال يحصد دعمًا جديدًا.. ويترقب مواجهات تاريخية في أفريقيا الهلال يحصد دعمًا جديدًا.. ويترقب مواجهات تاريخية في أفريقيا مباريات اليوم نجوم الهلال السوداني (FaceBook/ Al Hilal S.C﻿) 28 أكتوبر 2026 الهلال يحصد دعمًا جديدًا.. ويترقب مواجهات تاريخية في دوري أبطال أفريقيا أسفرت قرعة دور المجموعات لدوري أبطال أفريقيا، عن مواجهات تاريخية لنادي الهلال السوداني، إذ أوقعته في المجموعة الرابعة إلى جانب أندية بيراميدز المصري، وحوريا كوناكري الغيني، والمغرب الفاسي. وسيتجنب "النادي الأزرق" مأزقا كان قد واجهه الموسم الماضي، حين تعارضت مواعيد جولاته الافتتاحية في البطولة الأفريقية مع مباريات المنتخب السوداني، في تصفيات ونهائيات كأس العرب "الدوحة 2026"، ما أرهق نجومه بسبب كثرة التنقلات. ويحظى الفريق السوداني هذه المرة بفرصة مثالية لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية؛ والتأهل للدور المقبل من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، نظرا لملاءمة جدول افتتاح مشواره مع مواعيد مباريات "صقور الجديان" أمام "أسود التيرانغا". مواجهات تاريخية بانتظار الهلال تنتظر الهلال مواجهات مرتقبة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا ؛ حيث يواجه للمرة الأولى في تاريخه أندية بيراميدز، وحوريا كوناكري، والمغرب الفاسي، مبتعدا عن فرق اعتاد ملاقاتها في النسخ الأخيرة مثل مولودية الجزائر، وصن داونز الغائب عن البطولة، والذي تكررت مواجهته معه كثيرا في السنوات الماضية. ليكون على موعد مع سجالات تاريخية في مغامرة استعد لها الفريق جيدا. بتعاقده مع المدرب الألماني جوزيف زينباور، كما ودعم صفوفه بمحترفين أجانب متميزين. اقرأ أيضًا شطة لـ winwin: الأهلي يحتاج للحذر.. والهلال لغز محير نتائج قرعة دوري أبطال أفريقيا 2027 والمجموعات وتفادى النادي الأزرق موقفا محرجا، كان قد تعرض له بالنسخة الماضية من مرحلة مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بتعارض مبارياته الافتتاحية مع مباريات المنتخب بتصفيات ونهائيات كأس العرب التي أقيمت بالعاصمة القطرية الدوحة، في العام 2026، ما تسبب في إرهاق لنجومه الدوليين، بالنظر إلى وجود 11 لاعبا من الفريق في قائمة المدرب كواسي أبياه. وسيحظى الفريق بفرصة مثالية بخوض نجومه بالمنتخب لمباراتين قويتين ضد المنتخب السنغالي، يومي 13 و16 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني المقبل، على ملعبي داكار وجنوب السودان، ليلتحقوا بعد ذلك بفريقهم لخوض الجولة الافتتاحية من مرحلة المجموعات أحد أيام 29/28/27 من نفس الشهر، ما يتيح لهم فرصة خوض مباريات تنافسية أفريقية قوية، قبل أن يستهلوا مهمتهم مع فريقهم بمرحلة المجموعات. كما سيخوض رفاق القائد محمد عبد الرحمن مباريات قوية بالدوري الرواندي، في ظل توقف المنافسات المحلية، ستسهم في تجهيزهم للمباريات التي تنتظرهم بالبطولة، حيث تخطط إدارة النادي للتقدم بعيدا، محددة نصف النهائي كطموح مبدئي، فيما حددت 2028 موعدا أسفرت قرعة البطولات الأفريقية عن مواجهات صعبة للأندية المصرية في دور المجموعات. حيث وقع الزمالك في مجموعة تضم الأفريقي التونسي، مولودية الجزائر، ويانج أفريكانز التنزاني، مما يتطلب استعدادًا قويًا لضمان التأهل. تبدأ مباريات الزمالك بمواجهة الأفريقي في نهاية نوفمبر، تليها مباراة مع مولودية الجزائر في ديسمبر، ثم يانج أفريكانز في يناير. 

أما بيراميدز، فقد أوقعته القرعة في مجموعة تضم الهلال السوداني، حوريا الغيني، والمغرب الفاسي، حيث سيبدأ مشواره بمواجهة المغرب الفاسي. 

في الكونفدرالية، يواجه الأهلي الرجاء المغربي، بالإضافة إلى أول أغسطس الأنجولي وأسكو دي كارا التوجولي. تبدأ مباريات الأهلي بمواجهة أول أغسطس في القاهرة، تليها مباراة مع أسكو دي كارا في توجو، ثم الرجاء في ديسمبر. هذه القرعة تعكس تحديات كبيرة للأندية المصرية في السعي نحو تحقيق النجاح في البطولات الأفريقية.
